extracted.intended_audience: periodical essayists and writers of short satirical/humorous pieces (literate public and critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing brief, pointed periodical essays and satirical pieces: how to concentrate thought, choose subject matter, avoid common vices (partisanship, calumny, unnecessary particulars), and which comic techniques to deploy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Sheet should be a kind of Treatise, and make out in Thought what it wants in Bulk: That a Point of Humour should be worked up in all its Parts; and a Subject touched upon in its most essential Articles, without the Repetitions, Tautologies and Enlargements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write short papers that are nevertheless complete: a single paper should present a full, coherent treatment of its central point (humour or moral) without padding. Anti-patterns: repetition, tautology, and gratuitous enlargement that waste a short form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate to the 'quintessence' (chymical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Essay-Writer must practise in the Chymical Method, and give the Virtue of a full Draught in a few Drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for extreme condensation — reduce large ideas to their essential, potent form so that short pieces deliver the force of longer works. Example commentary: 'Were all Books reduced thus to their Quintessence, many a bulky Author would make his Appearance in a Penny-Paper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and public purpose of periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Our common Prints would be of great Use were they thus calculated to diffuse good Sense through the Bulk of a People, to clear up their Understandings, animate their Minds with Virtue, dissipate the Sorrows of a heavy Heart, or unbend the Mind from its more severe Employments with innocent Amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short humorous pieces should aim not only to amuse but to instruct and improve public understanding and morals; combine entertainment with the diffusion of good sense. Biblical/allusive support (Proverbs) is used as justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and accept your audience; don't write for 'moles'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not ... for the Benefit of Moles that I publish these my daily Essays. ('Spectacles ... could be of no use to a Mole.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some readers (ignorant or willfully envious) will not understand or appreciate the work; aim at sensible readers and be undisturbed by those who 'throw aside' your works. Anti-pattern: attempting to please every reader, including those incapable of appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid party spirit and partisan writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A furious Party Spirit ... exerts itself in Civil War ... and when it is under its greatest Restraints naturally breaks out in Falshood, Detraction, Calumny, and a partial Administration of Justice. Books are valued upon the like Considerations: An Abusive Scurrilous Style passes for Satyr, and a dull Scheme of Party Notions is called fine Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from partisan bias in essays: do not let party zeal or factional interest determine praise or condemnation. Evaluate and write on merit, truth, and equity rather than party alignment. Anti-patterns: using abuse as 'satire' or promoting party-talk as quality writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base writing on scandalous or unproven gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one Piece of Sophistry practised by both Sides, and that is the taking any scandalous Story that has been ever whispered or invented of a Private Man, for a known undoubted Truth ... Calumnies that have been never proved, or have been often refuted, are the ordinary Postulatums of these infamous Scriblers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid building essays or arguments on rumours, whisperings, or refuted calumnies. Treat such material as unreliable and unethical; using it is an anti-pattern that degrades the moral purpose of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve particulars/personalities except for exceptional occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Though you have taken a Resolution ... to avoid descending to Particularities of Dress, I believe you will not think it below you, on so extraordinary an Occasion, to Unhoop the Fair Sex, and cure this fashionable Tympany ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule avoid mean or petty particulars (personal attacks, minute dress-details), but allow targeted particulars when the occasion justifies it (an extraordinary or widespread absurdity). Maintain principled restraint; descend to particulars only when it serves public good or clear satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedic techniques: analogy, hyperbole, metaphor, classical allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter on the Hoop Petticoat uses architecture ('contrary to all Rules of Architecture widen the Foundations'), historical analogy (Alexander's armour), hyperbole (a Petticoat within some Yards of a modish Circumference), and simile (comparing a fashionable lady to a 'Black Monkey Enshrined').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid analogies, historical/classical allusions, hyperbole, and playful metaphors to expose absurdities and create humor. Examples in text model how to transform an observation into effective satire by comparison and exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer timelessness over ephemeral fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Masters in Painting never care for drawing People in the Fashion; as very well knowing that the Headdress, or Periwig, that now prevails ... will make a very odd Figure, and perhaps look monstrous in the Eyes of Posterity. For this Reason they often represent an illustrious Person in a Roman Habit, or in some other Dress that never varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, frame characters, types, and critiques in ways that will endure; avoid anchoring your piece entirely to passing fashions that will age badly. Use archetypes or classical framing to create lasting satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete anecdotes and local observation to illustrate wider truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes such as Sir Roger's schoolboy trick to avoid offending partisans when asking for Anne's Lane, or accounts of country party-humour (refusal to take a bettor), are used to display broader social follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground essays in short, specific anecdotes and local observations to reveal general social or moral points. Concrete stories make satire credible and enable the reader to infer the larger critique; anti-pattern: abstract moralizing without illustrative detail.
